column3: A riverside promenade in Shanghai. On one side stand old banks and trading houses in grand European styles, and on the other, the glittering towers of Pudong.
A TV tower in Pudong with large pink glass spheres, which became a symbol of modern Shanghai in the 1990s.
At 632 meters, one of the tallest buildings in the world, twisting as it rises, with a high observation deck.
A Ming-dynasty garden in old Shanghai, with rockeries, ponds, a zigzag bridge and a busy bazaar around it.
The most famous shopping street in China, with department stores, old brands and a busy walking street.
A maze of old lanes in Shanghai turned into small shops, studios and cafés.
A museum of ancient Chinese art, with famous collections of bronzes, ceramics, calligraphy and paintings.
A water town with canals, stone bridges and old shops, within the Shanghai area, so it is an easy day trip.
A large theme park in Pudong, with a castle and rides, with its own Chinese touches, such as a garden of the zodiac.
A Buddhist temple more than 1,700 years old that now stands among skyscrapers and shopping malls.
Small steamed dumplings with thin skins and a pocket of hot, savory soup. Bite a little hole and sip the broth first.
Pan-fried pork buns with a crisp golden bottom and soup inside, sprinkled with sesame seeds and scallions.
Shanghai's version of braised pork belly is sweet, rich and glossy with soy sauce and sugar.
Simple noodles tossed with fragrant fried scallion oil and soy sauce, a beloved Shanghai comfort food.
The local style of Shanghai cooking, with rich, sweet and savory dishes that use lots of soy sauce and sugar.
Hairy crabs, which are in season in the autumn, are steamed and eaten with ginger vinegar and rice wine, with sweet, creamy roe.
A glutinous rice roll with a crisp fried dough stick inside, with pickles, a classic Shanghai breakfast.
Haipai is the blend of Chinese and Western influence that shaped Shanghai's fashion, food and art.
An opera sung in the Shanghai dialect, telling stories of daily life in the city.
The qipao is a fitted dress with a high collar and side slit that became fashionable in Shanghai in the 1930s.
Lane houses with a stone-framed gate and brick walls, a style that mixes Chinese courtyard homes with Western terraces.
The tomb of Sun Yat-sen on Purple Mountain, reached by 392 steps. The blue-tiled hall stands among tall trees.
The tomb of the first Ming emperor, with a Sacred Way lined with stone animals and officials, in a forest of Purple Mountain.
A Confucius temple and the busy lantern-lit district around it along the Qinhuai River, with snack stalls, boats and old houses.
The longest surviving city wall in the world, built in the Ming dynasty, with huge brick gates and walkways.
A set of old government buildings and gardens, used by the Taiping rebel leader and later by Sun Yat-sen and the Republic.

column3: A memorial museum for the victims of the 1937 Nanjing Massacre, a solemn place for remembrance and peace.
One of the largest museums in China, with jade, bronzes and fine paintings in a big palace-style building.
Nanjing's famous cold duck is cured in salt and gently simmered, so its skin is pale and the meat tender and fragrant.
Glass noodles in a hot soup with duck blood, tofu and giblets, a beloved snack in Nanjing.
Small steamed dumplings from Nanjing, thin-skinned and juicy, often eaten with vinegar.
Small dishes sold along the Qinhuai River, such as duck oil pancakes, sweet rice balls and sesame cakes.
Yunjin is a rich silk brocade woven with gold thread for the imperial court, and woven on huge looms by two people.
A lantern show along the Qinhuai River at New Year, with thousands of lights in animal and legend shapes.
The largest of Suzhou's classical gardens, with ponds, pavilions and winding paths, built in the Ming dynasty. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
A garden of the Ming and Qing periods, with rockeries, halls and long covered walkways, and fine windows.
A hill with a leaning pagoda about a thousand years old, a symbol of Suzhou.
A quiet lane beside a canal with old homes, teahouses and small shops, and a taste of old Suzhou.
A famous water town, with canals, arched stone bridges and old wooden houses, often called the first water town of China.
A quieter canal town, with three bridges that locals once crossed on a wedding day for luck, and old merchant mansions.
A temple made famous by a Tang poem about a traveler hearing its bell at night while moored by a bridge.
A mandarin fish scored and fried so it curls like a squirrel's tail, covered in a sweet and sour sauce.
Suzhou noodles are served in a clear, sweet broth, with toppings such as braised pork or shrimp.
A sweet sticky rice porridge with brown sugar, sold by street vendors early in the morning.
The most famous brand of lake crab, from Yangcheng Lake near Suzhou, prized for sweet, rich meat.
Suzhou embroidery is very fine, with silk threads split thinner than hair, and can show a different picture on each side.
Kunqu is one of the oldest forms of Chinese opera, with slow, graceful singing and movements. It is a UNESCO-listed heritage.
Pingtan is a Suzhou storytelling art, with a performer or two telling tales in song, accompanied by a lute and pipa.
A giant standing bronze Buddha 88 meters tall that looks out over Lake Tai, next to a large temple.
A stretch of the Grand Canal with old streets, bridges and boats, where Wuxi's history can be explored.
Pork ribs braised in a sweet soy sauce until the meat comes off the bone, a Wuxi classic.
Wuxi's soup buns are sweeter than those in other regions, with a thin skin and juicy filling.
Hand-made clay figures from Huishan, painted in bright colors, a folk craft with a long history, such as chubby children and opera characters.
A narrow, winding lake in Yangzhou with a white pagoda, arched bridges and willows, said to be as graceful as a slender lady.
A garden famous for its four rockeries, which stand for the four seasons, among bamboo.
The original egg-and-ham fried rice, with shrimp and peas, known all over the world. The grains are separate and fluffy.
Big, soft pork meatballs that are simmered in broth with vegetables, said to look like a lion's head with its mane.
Steamed buns filled with chicken, pork and bamboo shoots, a classic of Yangzhou's tea houses.
One of the four great regional cuisines of China, known for fine knife skills, light flavors and fresh ingredients.
A storytelling tradition in which a single performer tells long stories with a fan and a gavel.
A temple on a hill beside the Yangtze in Zhenjiang, and the setting of the legend of the White Snake.
A dark, mellow rice vinegar, aged for months, one of the best-known vinegars in China.
Noodles cooked under a wooden pot lid, with a firm, springy texture, a Zhenjiang specialty.
Pork pressed and cured and set in clear jelly, eaten cold with ginger and Zhenjiang vinegar.
Strips of radish salted and dried in the sun, a crunchy pickled side dish.
Handmade wooden combs, a Changzhou craft that was a gift to the imperial court.
Blue-and-white cloth printed with patterns using a resist paste, a Nantong folk craft.
Fresh fish, crabs and shellfish from the Yellow Sea, cooked simply in Nantong's seafood restaurants.
Chicken braised in an iron pot over a fire with a flatbread stuck to the side of the pot to soak up the sauce.
Braised pork served with rice, a local favorite in the Xuzhou area, cooked slowly in soy sauce.
A mountain said to be the home of the Monkey King in Journey to the West, with caves and waterfalls.
Laver seaweed from the coast of Lianyungang, dried into sheets and used in soups and snacks.
Seafood from the Yellow Sea, served fresh in the port city of Lianyungang.
Fresh small river shrimp, boiled or stir-fried quickly, with a clean sweet taste.
A famous Huai'an dish of eel, cooked until it is soft and tender, and served in a savory sauce.
Thin crisp fried dough twists, eaten with tea as a snack in Huai'an.
A well-known baijiu from Yanghe in Suqian, with a mellow, sweet taste.
A long, slow morning meal of small buns and dim sum with pots of tea, a Jiangnan custom.
